claims.text: Equal-atomic NbMoTaW is a single-phase BCC refractory high-entropy alloy.
Equal-atomic NbMoTaW has excellent mechanical performance at 1600 °C.
Equal-atomic NbMoTaW has very poor room-temperature ductility.
NbMoTaW has irradiation resistance predicted by first-principles calculations.
Adding a few atomic percent Ti to NbMoTaW will improve its room-temperature ductility.
A representative intervention is 5 at.% Ti replacing equal shares of Nb, Mo, Ta, and W.
Ti can be uniformly distributed within the BCC matrix after vacuum arc melting and homogenization.
Low-level Ti addition enhances grain-boundary cohesion in NbMoTaW without changing the overall BCC lattice.
Ti atoms preferentially segregate to grain boundaries and interfaces in NbMoTaW.
Ti segregation reduces stress-concentration sites and facilitates room-temperature dislocation movement.
The Ti-induced bonding modification improves room-temperature plasticity.
A few atomic percent Ti will leave high-temperature strength largely unaffected.
A few atomic percent Ti will leave irradiation defect evolution and irradiation resistance largely unaffected.
Untreated NbMoTaW has approximately 2–4% room-temperature plastic strain.
Ti-doped NbMoTaW could exceed 10% room-temperature plastic strain.
Ti-doped NbMoTaW will retain yield strength at 1600 °C comparable to untreated NbMoTaW.
Ti-doped NbMoTaW will have irradiation resistance similar to untreated NbMoTaW.
The beneficial effect is limited to Ti concentrations low enough to preserve the single-phase BCC structure.
Excessive Ti or improper heat treatment may form secondary phases or reduce high-temperature performance.

contradictions.description: The intervention specifies that Ti is uniformly distributed within the BCC matrix, whereas the proposed mechanism requires Ti to preferentially segregate to grain boundaries and interfaces. The intended post-processing Ti distribution is therefore internally inconsistent or insufficiently qualified.
